description: Small team from Korea taking on the Dancing with the SARs challenge. We are interested in Earth observation, radar data and data visualization. Our team members are already set.
summary:
Ground Shift is a free, open web map for investigating NISAR L-band backscatter changes around two large development areas in Korea, which share one NISAR frame. At Saemangeum, tidal flats behind a 33.9 km sea wall are being reclaimed for land, roads and a port. At Yongin, hills and farmland are being graded for semiconductor clusters.

Users can play through 18 radar dates (Oct 2025 – Nov 2026), compare dates with a swipe slider and Before/After selectors (also on phones), switch between six layers (colour composite, HH, HV, change, a strict "persistent brightening" test, and a NASA HLS optical reference), and open evidence cards with the radar time series and radar/optical crops of each candidate patch.

The radar test uses no construction boundaries as input. We checked its candidates against a second, independent NASA dataset, HLS. At Saemangeum, candidate cells changed in the optical indices far more often than nearby comparison cells. At Yongin, the largest patches fall inside the chip-cluster construction site mapped on OpenStreetMap, but the optical check is inconclusive because of monsoon clouds. We report exploratory comparisons, not detection accuracy.
details:
What it does

  • Timeline: a time-true timeline of the 18 acquisitions we found for descending track 133, frame 70. Gaps are marked: no acquisitions in our set from Jan 18 to Jun 23, 2026, and the NISAR instrument gap from Jul 27 to Aug 10, 2026.
  • Product maturity: each date is tagged BETA (uncalibrated), PROVISIONAL or VALIDATED, read from each granule with its processing ID. The trend chart breaks its line at the BETA boundary, and the compare view warns when two dates come from products of different maturity.
  • Six layers: (1) RGB composite HH / HV / HH(dB)−HV(dB); (2) HH; (3) HV; (4) HH change versus Jun 23, 2026, the first PROVISIONAL date (not drawn for BETA dates); (5) persistent HH brightening: a pixel passes when HH is ≤ −8 dB on all three summer dates (Jun 23, Jul 5, Jul 17) and ≥ −3 dB on all three autumn dates (Oct 9, Oct 21, Nov 2); (6) NASA HLS true-colour seasonal references, summer (Jun 1 – Jul 31, 2026) and autumn (Oct 1 – Nov 2, 2026). These are seasonal composites, not imagery acquired on the selected radar date.
  • Evidence cards: the largest 12 patches per site have coordinates, area, the patch-median HH on all 18 dates, and paired radar and HLS crops with the patch outlined. Each card gives the optical index class with its denominator and the number of clear observations, and flags single-observation evidence. All candidates can be downloaded as GeoJSON.
  • Story panel: for each site, what brighter and darker radar can mean there, why the change matters, sourced facts about the projects, and the optical result.

How it works

  • We search the ASF DAAC for NISAR L2 GCOV products over both sites. Each file is about 6 GB; we read only the HDF5 chunks inside each study area over HTTPS with Earthdata Login, so no full download is needed.
  • Radar processing: 5×5 boxcar filter (a 50 m window) on linear power in the native 10 m UTM grid; area-averaged reprojection to 0.00025° (about 28 m × 22 m) and conversion to dB; one fixed colour stretch for all radar dates, which does not remove calibration or processing differences across product maturities.
  • The candidate test is deliberately strict: all six dates must exist and agree. Patches use 8-connectivity and a minimum of 4 pixels. Thresholds were set once from typical HH levels and were not tuned against construction maps.
  • Optical cross-check: our script reads only the study-area windows of NASA HLS v2.0 (L30 and S30) Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. Cloud, cloud shadow, adjacent cloud, snow and high-aerosol pixels are removed on each scene's own grid before reprojection. Per-observation NDVI and MNDWI medians give descriptive index classes, not land-use labels.
  • Optical results (exploratory, not accuracy). Comparison cells met the same summer radar rule, failed the autumn test, and lie within 2 km of a candidate; they are not matched on land cover, so we compare rates within the same summer optical state. At Saemangeum, all 59 candidate cells that looked water-like in summer had lost that signal by autumn, against 9.5% of 52,720 comparison cells; 63 of 136 vegetated candidate cells (46%) lost the vegetation signal, against 3.2% of 93,749. At Yongin only 11 of 34 candidate cells could be assessed (monsoon clouds), so the result is inconclusive. An earlier single-threshold rule also responded to seasonal harvest in comparison cells; we revised the classes after inspecting those results and document both.
  • The site is static HTML/JavaScript (Leaflet) on GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/nodora-lab/nisar-ground-shift (Apache-2.0). To add a new place, update scripts 01, 02 and 03 and the site content, then rerun processing.

Benefits and intended impact

Residents, journalists, teachers and local planners can explore radar changes possibly linked to land development, for free and through clouds, and check them against optical imagery in the same place. Saemangeum's tidal flats were a major stopover for migratory shorebirds; large industrial sites change water, traffic and land for whole towns.

We put the limits up front:

  • BETA data is uncalibrated, and "VALIDATED" refers to the NISAR product's maturity, not to our test.
  • The radar test combines PROVISIONAL and VALIDATED products, so processing differences may contribute to what it flags.
  • Radar brightness is not land use. Hectare figures count pixels that passed a test, not measured footprints. False-positive rates have not been measured.
  • Optical index rules also respond to harvest, drainage, seasonal conditions and mixed pixels; seasonal composites cannot date a change; neighbouring resampled cells are not independent samples.
  • The optical classes were revised during exploration and have not been tested on another area or period.

Tools

Python and JavaScript. Python libraries: asf_search, earthaccess, h5py, fsspec, rasterio, pyproj, scipy, Pillow. Web map: Leaflet. Design: Figma. Hosting: GitHub Pages.

Use of SI

We used SI assistants (Claude and ChatGPT) to help draft code and English text, to check facts against public sources, and to review the project as a mock judge. The team reviewed all of it. All radar overlays come from real NISAR data, and all optical overlays from real NASA HLS data, processed by the scripts in our repository. No SI-generated imagery is used in the map views or in the demo video.
